questions.q: What is the difference between a functional and a non-functional requirement?
keyPoints: Functional = what the system does: a specific behaviour or feature (e.g. 'a teacher can record a grade')
Non-functional = how well it does it: a quality attribute like speed, security, reliability, usability
Think FUN vs PERF: functional is the verbs/features, non-functional is the adjectives and numbers
Security counts as non-functional even though users don't 'see' it
questions.explanation: Same system, two questions: what does it do, versus how well does it do it.

questions.q: Why must every requirement be measurable and testable, and what makes one 'strong'?
keyPoints: A testable requirement can be checked at the end for a clear yes/no
'The system should be fast' is untestable and unprovable
A strong one has acceptance criteria: a metric, a condition, and how you'd verify it (e.g. 'p95 load under 300ms at 200 users, verified by load testing')
Vague requirements make it impossible to later prove you succeeded
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are the single biggest mark-earner in requirements.

questions.q: Why is feasibility assessed before a project starts, and what does each dimension ask?
keyPoints: It's an honest go/no-go check that the solution can realistically be delivered within constraints
Technical: do we have the skills, tools and technology to build it at all?
Economic: do the benefits justify the cost (cost-benefit / ROI)?
Cost-and-schedule: can we finish on time and budget, with a risk buffer? Operational: will people actually adopt it?
questions.explanation: You can have perfect requirements for a system you have no chance of delivering.

questions.q: Why do projects define boundaries, and what problem do they prevent?
keyPoints: Boundaries state what is in scope, out of scope (with a reason), and future scope
They defend against scope creep: the slow, uncontrolled addition of 'just one more feature'
When a stakeholder asks for something new, you point to the boundary doc ('that's phase two')
Unbounded scope blows deadlines and collapses quality (e.g. Denver airport baggage system)
questions.explanation: Boundaries aren't bureaucracy; they protect the schedule you said was feasible.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a data dictionary in software design?
keyPoints: It documents every data field: name, data type, whether required, constraints, and a description
Its purpose is to remove ambiguity before building, so everyone shares one view of the data
Choosing the right type matters (Decimal for money to avoid rounding; Date for date arithmetic)
It becomes the database schema you later build - a design tool, not end-of-project paperwork

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: Why should a developer design the algorithm before writing code?
keyPoints: You express the logic in a language-independent form (pseudocode, flowchart, structure chart) first
This lets you reason about and verify the logic before the syntax gets in the way
Logic errors are far cheaper to fix on paper than after code is written - the shift-left principle
The trap is jumping straight to code because you can; modelling is the blueprint the build follows

questions.q: How does the Waterfall approach differ from Agile?
keyPoints: Waterfall is sequential: each phase finished and signed off before the next ('falls once'), heavy documentation, feedback only near the end
Agile is iterative: short time-boxed sprints each delivering working software ('goes around'), with continuous client feedback and lighter, evolving docs
Waterfall is predictable but rigid; Agile is adaptable but has less predictable final scope and cost
Waterfall suits stable, regulated projects; Agile suits uncertain, fast-moving ones
questions.explanation: Waterfall Falls once; Agile Goes around - the central contrast of the chapter.

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: Why is Waterfall well-suited to a regulated medical or government system but not a startup app?
keyPoints: Regulated systems have stable requirements and mandatory, auditable documentation - Waterfall's exact strengths
Predictability is valued over speed, and late change is rare, so the rigidity costs little
A startup app has uncertain requirements that evolve with user feedback and a fast-moving market
Waterfall's 'falls once' rigidity and late feedback would make change expensive and risk building the wrong thing
questions.explanation: 'Waterfall is always bad' is the trap; it's right for the stable and regulated.

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: What is the WAgile hybrid, and how do you decide when to use Waterfall versus Agile behaviour within it?
keyPoints: WAgile = Waterfall stage-gates on the outside + Agile sprints inside each stage ('plan big, build small')
Gates give governance, predictability and documentation; sprints give flexibility and feedback
Apply Waterfall behaviour where governance dominates (compliance, formal reporting, predictable milestones)
Apply Agile behaviour where adaptability dominates (changing requirements, essential user feedback) - e.g. run the regulated core Waterfall-heavy, the user-facing app Agile-heavy
questions.explanation: Done badly it's the worst of both; you must justify the 'when and how', not just say 'it combines both'.

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: In the project management triangle, what happens if a client adds scope but refuses to move the deadline?
keyPoints: Scope, Time and Cost are interdependent, with quality squeezed in the middle - change one and the others must move
Fixing time while increasing scope forces cost up (more people) or quality down (cut testing/polish)
If neither cost nor quality is allowed to give, the deadline will slip in reality regardless
The right response is to make the trade-off explicit and negotiate (defer, drop a feature, or extend)

questions.q: What is the critical path, and why does a slip on it matter more than a slip elsewhere?
keyPoints: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the minimum possible project duration
Its tasks have zero slack: delay one and the whole project slips by the same amount
Non-critical tasks have slack and can be delayed within it without moving the finish date
So when a Gantt task slips, the answer depends entirely on whether it's on the critical path

questions.q: How do the implementation (changeover) methods trade off risk against cost?
keyPoints: Direct/big-bang: cheapest and fastest but highest risk - no fallback if it fails (Knight Capital, Denver)
Parallel: safest - old system runs as a live fallback and lets you verify outputs - but most expensive (two systems at once)
Phased and Pilot sit between; match the method's risk profile to the scenario's stakes
Key distinction: Phased splits by feature (rolled out to everyone gradually); Pilot splits by user group (whole system to a small group first)
questions.explanation: Direct is cheap and risky; Parallel is safe and costly - the two ends of the trade-off.

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: What is the difference between quality assurance and testing?
keyPoints: QA is the overall process: standards, reviews, criteria and continual checking across the whole project - it prevents defects
Testing is one activity within QA: running test cases against the built software to detect defects
Testing asks 'does this code work?'; QA asks 'do we have a process ensuring the whole solution meets its standards?'
QA prevents, testing detects; testing is one tool QA uses
questions.explanation: Conflating the two is the classic lost mark on this dot-point.

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: How does a developer genuinely involve and empower a client, rather than just gathering requirements once?
keyPoints: Treat the client as an ongoing partner, not a one-off source at week one
Involve: regular demonstrations of working software plus co-design so they help make decisions
Empower: give their feedback real influence over the product, not just informing them after the fact
Negotiate new requests around the Scope-Time-Cost triangle: clarify the real need, assess impact, offer options, document the agreement
questions.explanation: Projects fail more often from poor communication than from technical impossibility.

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: Why must real security live in the back end rather than the front end?
keyPoints: The front end can be bypassed - anyone can call the API directly - so it can never be trusted for security
Authentication, authorisation, input validation, parameterised queries and password hashing must sit on the server
The back end is the actual security boundary of the whole system
It must also fail securely: log error detail internally but return a generic message, so stack traces don't leak structure to attackers
questions.explanation: Treating the back end as invisible plumbing is the trap that gets projects breached.

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: What is the role of version control, and how does rollback act as a safety net?
keyPoints: Version control (Git) tracks all changes with a recoverable history, letting many developers work via branches and reviewed merges
Discipline: commit small, branch per feature, never commit to main; pull requests are review gates
Tagged releases (semantic versioning: major breaks, minor adds, patch fixes) let you return to exactly what was running
Rollback = redeploy the last known-good tag when a deployment fails - recovering in seconds
questions.explanation: Knight Capital lost $440M in 45 minutes partly because it had no rehearsed rollback.

source.ref: Generated from Software Engineering Project episode scripts

questions.q: What is the difference between boundary testing and path testing?
keyPoints: Boundary testing checks values at the edges of a valid range (just below, on, just above) where off-by-one errors hide - it's black-box, from the spec
For a 1-50 range you'd test 0, 1, 2, 25, 49, 50, 51
Path testing exercises every execution route: each branch true and false, loops at zero/one/many - it's white-box, needing to see the code
Together they catch the two big bug families: wrong logic on an untested branch, and errors at a limit
questions.explanation: Test every road through (path), and test the edges (boundary).

questions.q: Why should feedback be prioritised by evidence rather than by the loudest voice?
keyPoints: Raw feedback is noisy and contradictory; the skill is turning it into defensible decisions (Collect, Synthesise, Act)
Triangulate across multiple sources (surveys, analytics, support tickets) before trusting a finding
Prioritise on an impact-versus-effort matrix: high-impact/low-effort changes are quick wins
One angry email for a niche feature loses to analytics showing 60% of users abandon signup
questions.explanation: Also a fairness issue - representative sampling stops you building only for the vocal few.

questions.q: Why is evaluating a solution more than showing 'it works'?
keyPoints: Evaluation is a justified judgement of effectiveness against defined criteria, with evidence and reflection - not just 'the program runs'
Criteria come from the requirements and QA quality criteria (correctness, usability, performance, security)
Evidence comes from testing (comparing actual output with expected output) and synthesised user feedback
Reflection covers maintainability, deployment readiness and lessons learned - and you report discrepancies honestly, not hide them
questions.explanation: No measurable criteria means nothing to evaluate against, which is why sloppy requirements make evaluation impossible.
